core_themes.name: Scale and variability of tenant fees
core_themes.claim: Letting agent fees charged to tenants are high, vary considerably between agents for broadly similar services, and are difficult for tenants to understand or compare.

core_themes.name: Weak tenant market power and misaligned incentives
core_themes.claim: Because landlords, not tenants, appoint and can negotiate with agents, tenants have little or no ability to negotiate, opt out of, or exert competitive pressure on the fees charged to them.

core_themes.name: Failure of existing transparency requirements
core_themes.claim: Despite the Consumer Rights Act 2015 transparency requirements, many agents still display fees inconsistently or not at all, leading to confusion between landlords and tenants and instances of double-charging.

core_themes.name: Financial and behavioural harm to tenants
core_themes.claim: High, repeated up-front letting fees cause financial hardship and debt for tenants, deter moving home, hinder saving for a deposit, and create an incentive for agents to encourage short-term tenancy churn.

core_themes.name: Banning fees to rebalance market power
core_themes.claim: The Government has chosen to ban letting agent fees paid by tenants, rather than lesser measures, because it recognises landlords' stronger market position and expects this to sharpen agents' incentives to compete on price and quality for landlords' business.

core_themes.name: Scope and exceptions of the ban
core_themes.claim: The ban will cover fees charged by agents, landlords and third parties alike so that tenants pay only rent and a refundable deposit, with limited exceptions such as capped holding deposits and charges arising from tenant-caused actions.

core_themes.name: Scottish precedent as supporting evidence
core_themes.claim: The long-standing fee ban in Scotland is cited as evidence that such a ban can operate with minimal negative effects on the sector, landlords, agents or renters, supporting the case for introducing a similar ban in England.

core_themes.name: Anticipated costs and benefits, including possible rent effects
core_themes.claim: The Government expects agents to reduce excessive or double-charged fees and absorb some costs rather than fully passing them to landlords, while acknowledging that some landlords may raise rents, and is exploring complementary measures such as capping deposits to further reduce tenants' upfront costs.

core_themes.name: Local authority (Trading Standards) enforcement
core_themes.claim: The ban will be enforced primarily by local authority Trading Standards, building on their existing enforcement role for redress scheme membership and transparency requirements.

core_themes.name: Potential lead enforcement authority
core_themes.claim: The Government is considering designating a lead enforcement authority, modelled on the Estate Agent sector's NTSEAT, to provide a central point of referral and more consistent enforcement, though this option is not yet decided.

core_themes.name: Tenant empowerment and education
core_themes.claim: Educating and empowering tenants to understand their rights and challenge non-compliant agents is presented as a key mechanism to reduce the enforcement burden on local authorities and secure compliance.

core_themes.name: Penalties and deterrence design
core_themes.claim: The Government is weighing whether non-compliance should be a civil or criminal offence and considering higher fines or banning orders, modelled on existing redress/transparency penalties and the Housing and Planning Act 2016, to deter agents from charging banned fees.
